title: cameraunlock pipeline conformance vectors
purpose: Executable form of the 'Check.' paragraphs in docs/porting-the-pipeline.md. A port runs these instead of re-deriving the numbers, and cameraunlock-core runs them against its own C++ and C# implementations so a change that moves a constant or reorders a step fails in core first.

position_processor.note: rot_* is the CENTERED, SMOOTHED physical head rotation before per-axis sensitivity and inversion, exactly what HeadTrackingSession feeds the pivot term.

euler_roundtrip.note: Build an orientation from YXZ Euler, decompose it back. A port with no quaternion type substitutes its own compose/decompose pair; the singularity is in the decomposition, not in the representation.

packet.note: ok=0 means the datagram was rejected as a complete pose+position sample; the pose and position fields are then meaningless. ok_rotation and ok_position are the verdicts of the rotation-only and position-only entry points, which carry their own length and finiteness guards - a single ok cannot show a guard missing from one of them, because the other two still reject.

session_rot.note: Datagram -> duplicate-sample filter -> PoseInterpolator -> TrackingProcessor. No recenter is wired: the tracker owns the centre.

session_pos.note: Datagram -> duplicate-sample filter -> PositionInterpolator -> PositionProcessor. No recenter is wired.

step_ops.step: One frame. Fields are the unit's step fields, plus optional 'repeat' (default 1), 'label', 'new' (interpolator units), 'bytes' (session units, omit for a frame with no datagram).
step_ops.ramp: Generator. Fields: dt, count, new_every (default 1), from {}, per_sample {}. Expands to 'count' steps where value = from + per_sample * floor(i / new_every) and is_new = (i % new_every == 0). Session units deliver a datagram on EVERY expanded step regardless of new_every, which is how a 250 Hz relay of a 30 Hz source is expressed.
step_ops.grid: Generator, euler_roundtrip only. Fields: yaw/pitch/roll each {from, to, step}. Expands to the full cartesian product.

step_refs: An assertion's 'at' / 'from' / 'to' is either an integer index into the EXPANDED step list, a step's 'label' (its first expanded index), or '<label>:last' (its last expanded index).

assertions.abs_at_most: |out[i].field| <= value for every i in [from, to]
assertions.abs_at_least: |out[i].field| >= value for every i in [from, to]
assertions.max_step: |out[i].field - out[i-1].field| <= value for every i in (from, to]
assertions.min_step: |out[i].field - out[i-1].field| >= value for every i in (from, to]. A floor on movement, which is how a flat spot is detected.
assertions.angular_travel_at_most: sum of |shortest_angle_delta(out[i-1].field, out[i].field)| over (from, to] <= value
assertions.orientation_roundtrip_max_error: For every step, the angle in degrees between the orientation built from the input Euler and the orientation built from the output Euler is <= value. Compares ORIENTATIONS, not Euler triples: at the poles the decomposition is not unique and comparing triples is wrong.

constants._note: Single source of truth. Changing any of these is a breaking change to every consumer; add a new field instead. Each entry names the C++ and C# symbol so a port can be traced back.

frame_interpolation_speed.note: Smoothing speed at smoothing=0. factor = 1 - exp(-speed * dt).

max_smoothing_speed.note: Smoothing speed at smoothing=1. speed = 50 - (50 - 0.1) * smoothing, clamped to [0.1, 50].

interval_blend.note: EMA blend for the sample-interval estimate.

default_sample_interval.note: 1/30, NOT 1/60. Used until the second sample establishes a measured interval.

extrapolation_decay_seconds.note: Smoothstep ease from the capped segment position back to 1.0.

limit_y_down.note: downward; a config exposing one vertical limit must mirror it into both

gimbal_lock_sin_threshold.note: NOT 1.0. sin(89.9 deg) is 0.9999985 so the general branch keeps everything still well conditioned, while a quaternion built at exactly 90 deg measures ~0.9999998 and takes the lock branch.

tracker_pivot_forward_default.note: Compensation OFF by default. When enabled the pivot vector is (0, 0, -TrackerPivotForward).

cm_to_meters.note: OpenTrack position fields are centimetres on the wire.

trailer_version_offset.note: byte >= 1 is valid; compare with >=, not ==, so a later version still parses

vectors.title: Yaw crossing +180 traverses the shortest arc
vectors.catches: A plain lerp between two samples straddling the seam. A real Lua port produced 87.5 at quarter-way instead of 177.5, and travelled 350 degrees instead of 10.

vectors.title: Yaw crossing -180 traverses the shortest arc
vectors.catches: A sign error in the delta: it passes one direction and fails the other, so both directions have to be run.

vectors.title: Roll crosses the seam too, and pitch must not
vectors.catches: A port that applies the shortest-arc treatment to yaw only. Roll wraps for the same reason yaw does; pitch comes from asin, is bounded to +/-90, and giving it the same treatment is wrong.

vectors.title: When samples stop, the output settles on the last REPORTED pose
vectors.catches: Clamping the segment position to 1 + max_extrapolation_fraction and then holding it. A 25 degree head turn renders as 37.5 and stays there forever. Frames are 1/128 s so the 0.25 s hold boundary lands on an exactly representable accumulated time.

vectors.title: A dropout shorter than the hold still reaches and keeps the 1.5x cap
vectors.catches: Trading the anti-judder behaviour away when fixing the stall. A dropped packet or two is still a live feed: retreating there pulls the camera backwards against a head that is still turning.

vectors.title: A jittery packet clock must not turn steady head motion into judder
vectors.catches: An interval estimate that tracks the last observed gap instead of an EMA over several (kIntervalBlend raised towards 1). The head here turns at a constant 0.25 degrees per frame and the samples arrive alternately 2 and 6 frames apart, which is what a relay does under load. Blended, the estimate stays near the mean and the output advances at a near-constant rate. Tracking the last gap makes the segment finish in two frames and then sit dead for four, so the same steady turn renders as a 0.56 degree lurch followed by three frames of nothing.

vectors.title: A tracker feed from cold produces no step larger than one inter-sample delta
vectors.catches: A default sample interval of 1/60 for a ~30 Hz tracker, and equally a port with no first-sample park: either makes the first segment reach progress 1.0 in half a sample period, extrapolate to the cap and come back. Native mods had that first-second jolt and Unity mods did not. The floor under the per-frame movement is what stops an all-zero output and a raw passthrough - neither of which interpolates anything - from passing on the upper bounds alone.

vectors.title: The interval estimate starts at 1/30 s, not 1/60
vectors.catches: A default sample interval of 1/60. The default is only ever read before a measurable gap between two samples replaces it, and the first sample parks the segment, so the ONE window in which it is observable is a second sample that arrives closer than kMinSampleInterval (1 ms) - the estimate is left at the default and the segment it advances is a real one. Half an inter-sample period is exactly how far ahead of the truth a 1/60 guess runs, so the frame that should read 2.49 reads 4.99 and the segment reaches the extrapolation cap in half the time.

vectors.title: The position interpolator generates the frames between samples, like the rotation one
vectors.catches: A position interpolator that hands the raw sample straight back. The rotation half has vectors of its own and the position half had none, so an interpolator reduced to `return raw` scored a clean sheet. A 32 Hz source driving 128 fps must produce four evenly spaced frames per sample, not one step and three flat ones.

vectors.title: Position extrapolation expires on the same wall clock as rotation
vectors.catches: The position half of the held-forever extrapolation. Rotation and position run separate copies of the same segment maths, so fixing one and leaving the other parks the camera 5 cm forward of where the head actually is whenever the samples stop, while the head rotation settles correctly. Frames are 1/128 s so the 0.25 s hold boundary lands on an exactly representable accumulated time.

vectors.title: The position interval estimate is blended too
vectors.catches: An interval estimate in the position half that tracks the last observed gap. The two interpolators carry kIntervalBlend separately, so the rotation vector cannot see a position-side regression - and this is the axis where it shows worst, because a lurch-then-freeze in position reads as the camera physically jumping rather than as a slightly uneven turn. Same shape as sample-interval-estimate-resists-packet-jitter: a constant 2.5 mm per frame of lean with samples arriving alternately 2 and 6 frames apart.

vectors.title: The position interpolator starts from the same 1/30 s guess
vectors.catches: A 1/60 default in the position half only. The two interpolators carry the constant separately, so a port that fixes one leaves the other reaching the extrapolation cap in half a sample period - a position wobble at the tracker rate while the head rotation is smooth, which is exactly how the rotation-side bug was first described.

vectors.title: Position clamps before AND after smoothing, so nothing pins after the head returns
vectors.catches: Clamping only the output. The smoothing state winds up far outside the limits and the output then sits pinned at the limit for hundreds of milliseconds after the head has come back. Sensitivity 10 drives the raw input to 5.0 m; with the pre-clamp the smoothing state can never exceed 0.30.

vectors.title: Z and Y clamp asymmetrically, and the first sample snaps
vectors.catches: Two things at once. A symmetric z clamp (negative z is the FORWARD lean and gets the generous 0.40 m budget; +z backward gets 0.10 m), and a missing first-sample snap - without it the first frame blends up from zero instead of landing on the clamped input.

vectors.title: The up and down vertical budgets are two separate numbers
vectors.catches: Transposing the two arguments of the vertical clamp. With the shipped defaults limit_y and limit_y_down are both 0.20, so a swap is invisible; this vector sets them apart (0.20 up, 0.05 down) and reads each direction. A transposed clamp gives 0.05 up and -0.20 down - the head that leans down clips into the player body and the head that looks up barely moves.

vectors.title: Decomposing at exactly +/-90 degrees of pitch keeps the heading
vectors.catches: Both halves of the gimbal bug. Reusing the general yaw formula in the lock branch returns atan2(0, 0) = 0 and discards the rotation; testing sinPitch >= 1.0 never fires because float error leaves it a shade under 1, so the degenerate general branch runs anyway. The last two steps carry roll INTO the pole, where the yaw and roll axes coincide and the decomposition has to fold one into the other: 30 of yaw with 40 of roll comes back as -10 with no roll. An implementation that hands the input triple back unchanged fails there, and the orientation comparison alone cannot catch it because both triples name the same orientation.

vectors.title: Worst-case round-trip error over a full orientation sweep stays at the precision floor
vectors.catches: A gimbal branch error anywhere in the range, including in ports with no quaternion type - a matrix-to-Euler decomposition has exactly the same degenerate case. One Rust port concluded 'not applicable, no quaternion conversion' and had a worst-case error of 1.5708 radians, a full right angle silently dropped. The comparison is between ORIENTATIONS, because at the poles the Euler triple is not unique - which on its own is also satisfied by handing the input straight back, so the sweep runs past a full turn on yaw and roll and bounds the OUTPUT to the canonical range every stage downstream assumes: yaw and roll within 180, pitch within 90.

vectors.title: Decomposition returns the canonical triple, not the one it was handed
vectors.catches: A decomposition that is not one - a harness or a port that echoes the Euler angles it was given. Comparing orientations cannot see that, because the echoed triple names the same orientation by construction. These inputs sit outside the canonical range every stage downstream assumes, so the correct output differs from the input: 200 of yaw comes back as -160, and -350 of roll as 10. A port whose interpolator then lerps 200 towards -160 travels the long way round the seam.

vectors.title: With pivot compensation on, a pure head turn produces zero pan
vectors.catches: A +z pivot vector. Rotation is linear, so R(-v) - (-v) == -(R(v) - v): building the pivot as +z computes the exact negation of the real artifact and subtracting it DOUBLES the phantom translation. The input here is exactly the artifact a 0.10 m pivot produces at 30 degrees of yaw, so the correct output is zero and a +z port outputs twice the artifact. The trailing phase rides a real 0.06 m lean on top of that same artifact and asserts it arrives, so a pipeline whose output is zero because nothing reaches it fails where a working one reports the lean.

vectors.title: Pivot compensation is off unless the mod turns it on
vectors.catches: A port that ships a non-zero default. The correct arm length is a property of the tracker app, not of this library - the Headcam Android app already applies its own eye-anchor offset while iOS applies none. This vector sets no pivot at all, so it reads the implementation's own default: the raw offset must pass through untouched even with the head rotated.

vectors.title: The pivot artifact is three-dimensional: pitch swings the head through both arms
vectors.catches: A compensation built on yaw alone, and one that ignores the upward arm. A tracker watching the eyes sees a point both ahead of and above the neck, so pitching the head moves it through an arc in the y-z plane that a yaw-only term leaves entirely uncorrected. The input here is exactly the artifact that a 0.10 m forward and 0.05 m upward pivot produces at 20 degrees of pitch, so the correct output is zero; a yaw-only implementation reports the whole 3.1 cm of phantom rise, and one that drops the upward arm reports what is left of it.

vectors.title: Deadzone subtracts in the input's direction rather than gating on it
vectors.catches: Gating. With a deadzone of 5, an input of 4.99 gives 0 and 5.01 gives 5.01, so a 0.02 degree movement pops the camera 5 degrees. The correct output for 5.01 is 0.01. All three axes carry the same input because pitch and roll have their own deadzone call sites, and a gate left in either of them is invisible to a yaw-only vector.

vectors.title: Diagonal head motion introduces no roll
vectors.catches: Quaternion SLERP substituted for per-axis Euler smoothing. Slerp follows the great circle between two orientations and that arc's Euler decomposition carries a non-zero roll term for compound movement, so diagonal head motion rolls the horizon. Remote smoothing is on so the smoother is genuinely lagging the input across the sweep. The per-frame floors on yaw and pitch are what stop a dead pipeline passing: a bound on roll alone is satisfied by an output that never moves at all.

vectors.title: 40.0 on the wire is 0.40 m out
vectors.catches: A missing cm-to-m conversion. Every position limit in this library is metric, so without the 0.01 factor a 4 mm lean saturates limit_z and position tracking degenerates into a three-axis on/off switch. Rotation fields are degrees on the wire and are NOT scaled.

vectors.title: Finiteness is checked AFTER narrowing to 32-bit float
vectors.catches: Validating the raw double only. A finite double can exceed the float range (1e300), and the narrowing cast then produces infinity, which poisons every downstream sin/cos and view-matrix computation with NaN. The socket binds INADDR_ANY, so any host on the network can send this.

vectors.title: A 54-byte trailered datagram delivers its pose like any other
vectors.catches: Rejecting the datagram on length, or reading the pose from the wrong offsets once a trailer is present. Bytes 0-47 are standard OpenTrack; the trailer is magic 'HCAM', a version byte compared with >= so a later version still parses, and a wrapping u8 counter.

vectors.title: A datagram shorter than the pose is rejected, not read past
vectors.catches: A missing length guard. The socket binds INADDR_ANY, so any host on the network can send a 24-byte datagram; without the check the parser reads 24 bytes past the end of the buffer and reports whatever was there as a head pose. Every entry point needs its own guard - the rotation parse, the position parse and the combined one are three separate functions and a port that guards one of them has two holes left.

vectors.title: Extra bytes past the pose are not a Headcam trailer
vectors.catches: Reading the trailer off length alone. Plain OpenTrack sends 56 bytes when it appends its frame counter, and byte 52 of that counter is not a version number - a parser that skips the magic check reports a trailer, latches a counter out of the middle of a double, and a port that ever acts on that recenters at random. The magic has to be checked, and a datagram carrying a truncated trailer (53 bytes) has to report no trailer while still delivering its pose.

vectors.title: A later trailer version still parses; version 0 does not
vectors.catches: Comparing the version byte with == instead of >=. The trailer is wire protocol and the version byte exists so a later Headcam build can add to it; an equality test makes every future version invisible to every already-shipped mod, which is the whole failure the version byte was added to avoid. Version 0 is not a trailer and must be rejected from the other side.

vectors.title: The trailer is parsed and then not acted on
vectors.catches: Acting on the trailer. The tracker owns the centre: it zeroes its own output before signalling, so with the mod-side centre at identity the zeroed stream is already correct. A port that recenters on the trailer captures (20, 10, -3) as a centre, and when the tracker's stream then drops to zero the output parks at the negated, mirrored centre instead of zero.

vectors.title: An uncentered rotation stream that drops to zero lands at zero, not at the negated offset
vectors.catches: Capturing the incoming pose as a centre when the connection comes up. That puts a SECOND centre in series with the tracker's own, and the two drift apart because each recenters at moments the other cannot see. At startup both are near zero and it looks fine; the symptom is the player pressing Center on a tracker that sends no trailer, the stream dropping to zero, and the view parking at the negated drift until they also press the mod's hotkey.

vectors.title: The same, for position - it is captured separately and a rotation-only test passes with this half broken
vectors.catches: A position centre captured on connect. 20.0 cm on the wire is 0.20 m, inside limit_x, so a port that subtracts a captured centre outputs -0.20 here rather than 0.

vectors.title: The estimated sample interval follows the SOURCE rate, not the packet rate
vectors.catches: Deriving 'is this a new sample' from a packet counter or a receive timestamp alone, with no comparison of the pose values. OpenTrack relays at ~250 Hz regardless of source rate, so the interval EMA collapses to the packet interval, each segment finishes within a frame or two of the sample that started it, and the inter-sample frames the interpolator exists to generate collapse into flat spots. Here 256 datagrams per second carry a value that changes only every 8th one, a 32 Hz source. With the filter the output climbs steadily at ~1 degree per frame all the way across each source period; without it it lurches on the frame the value changes and then crawls, so the floor on the per-frame movement is what separates them.
